title: docs: say plainly what the ZK predicates are waiting on
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39, #40 and #41.** Cut from `feat/vac-invocation`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `114a050`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## Why

The Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure section lists the predicates the schemas are deliberately shaped to support, then closes with *"Detailed ZK protocols and registry-ZK interactions are left to future work."* A reader cannot tell from that which predicates are constructible today, which depend on work nobody has done, or where that work lives. The predicate list reads like an inventory of available machinery. It is not one.

That gap gets worse as the catalogue grows. #19 added two delegation predicates, #29 added two more for authority, and the correlation-scope change altered when the oldest of them needs the missing primitive at all. Four separate PRs each added a line to a list whose status nobody had stated.

## What the note says

**One primitive carries four predicates.** A proof that two credentials, or two identifiers, are under common control, without disclosing either. No DTG specification defines it. It is tracked in #9, and it carries:

- the community-anchored proof, wherever a party's VMC identifier and its VRC identifier differ;
- the shared-subject requirement that stops two parties pooling one's membership with the other's authority;
- proving a VDC chain valid without disclosing it;
- proving a VAC chain valid without disclosing it.

**Declared scope promoted the first of these from edge case to ordinary case.** A member who declares `pairwise` toward their community and `pairwise` toward a counterparty holds two identifiers that differ by construction, so a community-anchored proof must cross them rather than read one identifier out of both credentials. The body already says this in the construction itself; the note makes the consequence for #9 explicit rather than leaving it to be inferred two sections apart. This is the point #31 flagged when it said #9 *"stays open, and gains weight"*.

**The unsalted digest binders sit with the same task force**, per #38, and now cover five members rather than the three that issue was filed against.

## The part I most wanted written down

**Nothing in this specification is unverifiable while that work is outstanding.** Every requirement here can be checked by presenting the credentials themselves, which is exactly what a holder must do today to satisfy any predicate in the list. The cost is privacy, not correctness, and it falls hardest where a chain is involved because the disclosure boundary is the whole chain rather than the credential presented.

So the note ends with a SHOULD NOT: implementations should not defer shipping a rule of this specification on the grounds that its zero-knowledge form is unspecified. Without that sentence, "left to future work" is readable as "this part is not ready", which is not true of any normative rule here.

## Scope

Editorial and informative. No normative rule changes, no schema changes. It replaces one vague bullet with a note that names the dependency, the issues tracking it, and the interim position.

title: feat: state that a VAC is not a bearer credential
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39 and #40.** Cut from `feat/vac-attenuation-limit`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `df222cb`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## The gap

The VAC had no counterpart to the VDC's [Invocation Binding](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29/files), which opens *"A VDC is not a bearer token"* and requires the presenter to demonstrate control of the subject's verification method. The VAC said nothing, and its `audience` field is OPTIONAL with its absence documented as meaning **any holder may present it**. So a VAC without `audience` was a bearer credential, and nothing in the specification recorded that as a decision rather than an omission.

Even with `audience` set, the field was unenforceable. It named the DID that must present the credential, but no rule required a verifier to establish that the presenter controlled it. A constraint with no check.

**This is sharper for a VAC than for a VDC**, because a VAC chain is presented in full on every use. A captured presentation is a captured chain. A specification that let a holder be identified by possession alone would make every verifier a distribution point for the authority it had just been shown.

## It also closes an inconsistency already in the text

[Relationship to Capability Models](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29/files) says the mechanics the VDC borrows from ZCAP-LD and UCAN are *"attenuation-only re-delegation, chains resolving to a recognized root, and binding to a demonstration of key control at invocation"*, and adds that *"chained permissions are the VAC's territory, and its Attenuation rules apply the same mechanics to authority."*

The VAC applied the first two. The third was never written down. So the specification already claimed this rule existed. This PR makes it true rather than adding something new, which is also why "is bearer intentional here?" has no good answer in the current text: both readings are supported, by different sections.

Worth noting that the comparison does not push the other way either. UCAN requires the invoker to sign the invocation and ZCAP-LD requires proof of control, so neither of the models cited is bearer at invocation.

## The rules

- A verifier MUST NOT accept a party as holding the authority a VAC confers unless that party demonstrates control of the verification method associated with the presented VAC's `credentialSubject.id`, at the time of the request.
- Where the presented VAC carries `audience`, the party that demonstrated control MUST be the DID it names. The two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other: key control establishes that the presenter is the subject, `audience` establishes that this subject is the one the issuer expected to be presenting here.
- **Only the presented VAC's subject demonstrates anything.** The links above it are not present and are asked for nothing. Requiring otherwise would defeat attenuation, whose whole purpose is that the party who attenuated is not in the loop when its agent acts.

How the demonstration is requested and carried is left to the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification, exactly as the VDC leaves it. That is the same dependency #11 tracks, and this PR adds no new one.

## Also in the diff

Security Considerations gain bearer use of a VAC. Conformance Target 3 gains the key-control rule alongside the chain and status rules. The `audience` schema text no longer says any holder may present, and the attenuation SHOULD explains what setting `audience` buys. CONTEXT.md follows.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: feat: define how authority is withdrawn from a VAC
body:
> **Stacked on #29.** This branch is cut from `feat/vac-authority-credential`, because the section it changes exists only there. Until #29 merges, the diff against `main` shows #29's commits too; the change under review is the single commit `5833d4f`. Draft until #29 lands, at which point this rebases onto `main` and is ready.

## The gap

A VAC could not be taken back other than by waiting, and `validUntil` was only RECOMMENDED — so a VAC issued without one conferred authority that nothing could ever withdraw. The schema said as much in passing (*"authority that does not expire is authority nobody can withdraw by waiting"*) without requiring anything of an issuer.

The [[VDC]] section works the same problem carefully: `validUntil` REQUIRED, `credentialStatus` CONDITIONAL on a governing freshness window, revocation latency in Security Considerations, status lookups as a correlation surface in Privacy Considerations. The VAC section had none of it.

**The gap is worse for a VAC than for a VDC, which is why this is worth a PR rather than an editorial pass.** A VDC has a remedy the VAC does not: its verifier re-asks the permission question of the delegator at the time of the act, so withdrawing the delegator's own authority stops every delegate at once without touching a single credential. A VAC *is* that answer rather than a pointer to it. Nothing about the subject's current standing is consulted at verification, so expiry and revocation are the only remedies that exist.

## What this adds

**`validUntil` REQUIRED has moved to #29**, since a working draft should not publish a rule under which a conformant VAC confers authority nothing can withdraw. That leaves expiry as the sole withdrawal mechanism in #29, which is coherent standing alone, and this PR adds revocation on top of it. #29 carries an editor's note pointing here.

**`credentialStatus` is CONDITIONAL** on the freshness window the party governing the scope defines, mirroring the VDC rule.

**A new `### Withdrawal` subsection.** Expiry is the primary mechanism: it costs a verifier no network access, discloses nothing, and cannot fail open or closed, so it is the only withdrawal mechanism that survives the offline verification the VAC is built around. Only a VAC's issuer may revoke it — an attenuating holder revokes what it issued, the governing party revokes what it issued, neither reaches the other's directly.

**The verification rule is self-describing, which is the design decision here.** A verifier MUST check the status of every link that carries `credentialStatus` and MUST reject the chain if any is revoked; a link carrying none is evaluated on its validity period alone, and its absence is not a defect. The alternative — a status check per link — would have cost the VAC the property #29 spent the most text defending. Network cost now stays proportional to what a chain actually claims: one check for a long-lived root over short-lived attenuations, none where every link is short-lived. The two examples show exactly that contrast, the six-month root gaining a `credentialStatus` and the four-hour agent attenuation carrying none.

**Revocation cascades, and the section says so in both directions.** Revoking a VAC withdraws everything attenuated from it, transitively, whether or not the revoking issuer knows those derivations exist. That is what makes attenuation safe to permit without the governing party's involvement: it withdraws the whole tree in one act and needs no register of what its holder went on to issue. The converse is stated as plainly rather than buried — a chain whose links carry no status cannot show that an ancestor was revoked, so a verifier will accept an attenuation whose parent was revoked an hour ago. Offline verification bounds that exposure by the shortest `validUntil` in the chain; it does not remove it.

## Everywhere else the VDC's rules already reach

- **Attenuation** gains a SHOULD for short validity, since an attenuating holder is often a person, a device, or an agent rather than an operator of a status list, and may be unreachable when its grant needs taking back.
- **Relationship to the VDC** no longer claims the VAC chain is wholly offline. It is precommitted, with status on the links that carry it as the one live dependency. Overstating this was a small inaccuracy in #29 that this change would otherwise have made larger.
- **Security Considerations** gain items 19 and 20: revocation latency, and the cascade together with its invisibility where status is absent.
- **Privacy Considerations** gain item 14. Status on a root gives back part of what bearer-side presentation bought: whoever hosts the root's status list learns that a verifier checked it and when, so a governing party observes the *timing* of activity by agents and devices it never issued to and cannot see. One lookup for a whole chain rather than one per link, and timing rather than content — but it is the honest reason the section prefers short validity to status wherever re-issuance is available.
- **Governance Considerations** gain item 7, which is also the first VAC entry in that list: action vocabularies, the status mechanism, the freshness window, and whether status is required outright, are the governing party's to define.
- **Conformance Target 3** covers the status-checking rule alongside the chain rule.
- **CONTEXT.md** and the glossary entry follow.

## Not in scope, deliberately

**Resolved in #40, stacked on this branch.** The asymmetry below is settled there: the defaults should differ, and the control is an opt-out (`maxAttenuation`) rather than the VDC's opt-in `maxDepth`. Left here for the record.

**Attenuation is permitted by default; re-delegation is not.** A VDC prohibits re-delegation unless `maxDepth` explicitly authorises it (*"Setting `maxDepth` above 0 is the delegator's explicit authorisation to re-delegate; there is no other"*). A VAC permits attenuation unconditionally, capped at depth 8. That asymmetry may well be right — attenuation only ever narrows, and the cascade rule this PR states means a governing party can always withdraw the whole tree — but it is a deliberate difference that neither section argues for, and a governing party currently has no way to say "this authority is not attenuable". Worth settling separately; withdrawal is the control it leans on in the meantime, which is part of why this PR matters.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors, and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: feat: add the VAC (verifiable authority credential)
body:
## What this adds

The **Verifiable Authority Credential (VAC)**: a credential whose issuer governs a scope and states which actions its subject may take there, **in the subject's own name**. It stands outside the three informative categories rather than founding a fourth, following the reasoning in #28. An empty `actions` array confers nothing; no action implies another.

A holder MAY **attenuate** a VAC — derive a narrower one for an agent, a device, or a session — without returning to the governing party. Verifiers walk the chain the holder presents, reject any link that widens what its parent conferred or that was not issued by its parent's subject, and never dereference `parent`. Chain depth is capped at 8.

## Why

The catalogue had no credential meaning *"the governing party has decided you may do X here"*, so implementations were packing permission into VEC endorsements. An endorsement is a statement *about* a party that a verifier weighs for itself; a VAC is a statement *to* a verifier by the party entitled to decide. The AI-agent case forces it: an agent should carry four hours of read-only access to one scope, not its principal's own standing.

## Rebased onto WD02 `main` (#27, #26, #30, #19)

This is the last PR in the #31 sequence, and its rebase carries the reconciliation only it can do:

- **Vocabulary.** Written in declared-scope terms; the issuer line no longer names C-DID or M-DID. The `community_did.md` edit is dropped (the file is gone), and the service-node editor's note is deleted rather than rewritten: under declared scope a mediator's identifier is simply a DID declared `public`.
- **`parent` by digest.** An attenuated VAC references its parent by digest per Digest Encoding, not by `id`, so every cross-credential reference in the spec takes one form and a `parent` names nothing a verifier could be induced to fetch. Digest Encoding records why the consent and attestation references need the digest and the chain references use it for uniformity.
- **VDC ↔ VAC.** The VDC's table row and prose saying authority is *"not defined in this specification"* now point at the VAC. The VAC is named as one of the things that satisfies check 2 of *How a Delegation Composes with Authority*, and *Relationship to Capability Models* notes that chained permissions are the VAC's territory. The VAC's editor's note quoting #19 becomes a **Relationship to the VDC** subsection stating the composition rule (reach = intersection), the verification-model difference (precommitted and offline vs. live at invocation), and a MUST NOT each way.
- **Which credential an agent's grant is** (review). An attenuated **VAC** when the agent acts *as itself*: the record shows the agent as the actor, and the chain is provenance of its authority, not attribution of its acts; nothing a PHC or VMC attests about the principal travels with it. A **VDC** when the act is to be attributed to the person. Cross-referenced from the VDC's *whose name?* test, so the two sections give one answer.
- **Placement (D-B).** The VAC is a standalone `##` section, as the review endorsed. Promoting the VIC alongside it, so that no section has exactly one subsection, is an outline change left to a small follow-up under #28; the placement note says so.

## Review items from @bmiller59

1. **Possession chain.** An attenuated VAC's `issuer` MUST be the `credentialSubject.id` of the VAC it attenuates, and a verifier MUST reject a chain in which any link fails that check. Stated in the attenuation rules, the verification paragraph, and Security Considerations.
2. **Top-level `id`** — retired rather than satisfied. `authority.parent` is now a digest per Digest Encoding, aligned with the VDC's `parent` and `accepts`, so nothing refers to `id` and it stays optional as for every other credential. The reasoning, including a review of every cross-credential reference in the spec, is in the thread below.
3. **ZK predicate list** gains the VAC chain predicate and the shared-subject predicate that *Authority and membership are separate credentials* already cross-referenced.

## D-C: the considerations lists, regrouped once

As proposed in #31, this PR restructures both lists under subheadings in a single commit so that later additions stop renumbering everything:

- **Security Considerations** (18 items): every credential / membership and invitation / delegation (VDC) / authority (VAC). Renumbered; nothing cited these by number.
- **Privacy Considerations** (13 items): identifiers and correlation / disclosure / delegation and authority chains. The items the VDC section cites by number (1, 3, 10, 12, 13) keep their numbers; only unreferenced items moved.

## Changes

- `spec/body.md` — VAC section (schema, two examples, attenuation, relationship to the VDC, authority ≠ membership); taxonomy diagram and type hierarchy; VDC reconciliation; VMC note that membership requires a collective; VIC editor's note resolved; ZK predicates; Security and Privacy regrouped; Conformance Target 3.
- `spec/header.md`, `spec/intro.md` — seven → eight types; the VAC outside the categories.
- `spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_authority_credential.md` — new. `dtg_node.md` — adds VTNs and services; the list is illustrative rather than closed.
- `CONTEXT.md` — VAC entry; the delegation-vs-authority entries updated.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors and JSON examples validated; every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: docs: promote the VIC to a top-level section (closes #28)
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39, #40, #41 and #42.** Cut from `feat/zkp-dependencies`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `aad2665`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## What this decides, and whose call it is

This implements **decision D-B of #31** along the third option recorded there, which was @geoffturk's stated lean: keep the semantic split, with the VDC an edge credential, and fix the outline editorially rather than by moving credentials between categories.

#31 is explicit that D-B *"is a WG call to make here, not a side effect of merging"*. This PR does not pre-empt that. It exists so the option has a diff to look at rather than a paragraph, and it is trivially closed if the group prefers one of the other two. Nothing in it is normative.

## The change

#28 exists to remove sections that have exactly one subsection. "Invitation Credentials" containing only the VIC was the original case that prompted it. The VAC arrived in #29 as a top-level section for precisely that reason, which left the VIC as the last one standing.

The VIC is now its own section, so neither credential is filed under a category invented to hold a single member. Two functional categories remain, **edge** and **annotation**, three credentials each:

| | |
|---|---|
| Edge | VRC, VMC, VDC |
| Annotation | VPC, VWC, VEC |
| Outside both | VIC, VAC |

The VIC sits outside because it bootstraps a node *into* a community rather than connecting or annotating nodes already in the graph, which is what the old one-member category was really saying. The VAC sits outside because it neither forms an edge nor annotates existing structure.

The taxonomy diagram, the introduction's category list and its "three categories" note, and the VAC's placement note all follow. The placement note becomes ordinary prose, since it no longer records an open question.

## One thing I went slightly beyond the ask for

"Formal W3C Type Hierarchy" was the last heading in the document that was an only child. Nothing linked to it, so it is now a labelled paragraph inside the taxonomy section. Leaving it would have satisfied #28's letter while breaking the rule it states, and I would rather not close an issue against a document that still contains an instance of what it describes.

Verified after the change: no section in the specification has exactly one subsection.

## Scope

Editorial. No normative rule changes, no schema changes, no reference changes, and every anchor and JSON example still validates. The categories are informative, so what this moves decides nothing about any credential.

title: feat: let a governing party bound or forbid attenuation of a VAC
body:
> **Stacked on #29 and #39.** Cut from `feat/vac-withdrawal`, because the section it changes exists only there. Until both land, the diff against `main` carries their commits too; the change under review is the single commit `c106e8c`. Draft until #29 and #39 merge, at which point this rebases onto `main`.

## The asymmetry

A [[VDC]] forbids re-delegation unless `maxDepth` explicitly authorises it — *"Setting `maxDepth` above 0 is the delegator's explicit authorisation to re-delegate; there is no other."* A VAC permits attenuation unconditionally, bounded only by the chain-depth ceiling of 8, which #29 is explicit is *"a resource bound, not a stylistic one"* — a denial-of-service control, not a policy one.

So a governing party could not decline to have an action re-granted, however sensitive it was. And neither section argued for the difference, which is what made it read as an oversight rather than a decision. It came up on #39 and this settles it.

## The defaults should differ, and now the specification says why

Extending the two chains does different things.

A further **delegation** adds a party who may act *in the principal's name*, so the principal has to keep the register of who can speak for it, and a delegate that needs help can ask the principal for a fresh root delegation. Failing closed costs little.

A further **attenuation** only narrows, and its subject acts *as itself*, so nothing new is attributed to the governing party or to the attenuating holder. More to the point: **forbidding attenuation does not stop a holder equipping an agent.** It makes them lend their own key instead, which confers everything they hold rather than a subset, lasts as long as their own authority does, and is indistinguishable to a verifier from the holder acting in person. Attenuation is the safer of the two things a holder will actually do, and a default that pushed holders toward the other would buy nothing.

That argument is why this PR does **not** simply copy `maxDepth` across.

## What it adds instead

**`authority.maxAttenuation` (OPTIONAL)** bounds how far a chain may extend below the VAC that carries it. `0` forbids attenuation outright, for an action sensitive enough that the governing party wants to decide personally who holds it. Absent means attenuation is permitted as far as the depth ceiling allows.

A link MAY lower a limit, or set one where its parent set none, and MUST NOT raise one — so the effective limit on a chain is the strictest any of its links imposes, in keeping with attenuation never widening what it derives from. A verifier MUST reject a chain in which any VAC lies more than *n* steps below an ancestor bearing `maxAttenuation` *n*.

**It is deliberately not called `maxDepth`.** One name that fails open in one credential and closed in the other is a mistake waiting to be made by an implementer who has read only one of the two sections. The section also states that the ceiling and this limit are separate controls and that a chain must satisfy both: five links under a root bearing `maxAttenuation` `2` is within the ceiling and still invalid.

## A second gap, surfaced by the first

The VAC had no counterpart to the VDC's third check (*"Must the delegate independently qualify?"*). A valid chain establishes that authority was narrowed by parties entitled to narrow it. It does not establish that the party now holding it is one the scope is willing to deal with — and because that party acts as itself rather than in its attenuator's name, it may be one the governing party has never encountered. A member granted write access could derive write access for an outside contractor, who then writes in the room as itself.

A governing party MAY now require the subject of an attenuated VAC to independently qualify, and a verifier enforcing that policy MUST reject a chain whose subject does not, however well formed the chain is. That is recorded as a governance determination alongside the equivalent one for delegates.

## Also in the diff

The agent example carries `"maxAttenuation": 0`, which is what equipping an agent ordinarily wants and shows the opt-out in place. Security item 15 gains the limit among its rejection reasons, the zero-knowledge chain predicate gains depth, and CONTEXT.md and the glossary entry follow.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: feat: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope (pairwise | directed | public)
body:
Closes #22. Closes #23.

Implements **[#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)**, which offered to write the text if the WG considered it in scope for WD02. Here it is, so the change can be judged as spec prose rather than as a proposal.

**Updated** to carry the resolution reached in [cred-tf discussion #41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41) and in [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22): **three** scope values, not four, and the four acronyms retired outright rather than kept as shorthand. What changed since the first push, and since review, is summarised at the bottom.

## The problem

Each of the four VID types encodes **two independent things in one name**: what the identifier is attached to, and how widely it may be correlated. Only the second is what implementers and users need to reason about — and the first is already carried by the credential the identifier appears in. A VMC's subject is a member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship. The credential says so.

Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where the ambiguity lives: put an M-DID in a VRC — which §VRC explicitly permits — and both names apply.

## The change

One axis, ordered, declared by the holder:

| Scope | Known to | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pairwise` | exactly one counterparty | R-DID; M-DID where the community is the only counterparty |
| `directed` | a set of counterparties the holder chooses | P-DID; M-DID where the member is deliberately correlatable |
| `public` | unbounded; ordinarily published so that it can be found | C-DID |

Plus the principle: **roles are conferred by credentials, scope is declared by the holder.**

### Why three and not four

Per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460210235) and [@geoffturk](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153). A `community` value was the only one whose bound came from **structure** (the VMC) rather than from the holder's choice — a role smuggled back onto the scope axis, which is precisely what this change exists to remove. It is also a distinction no verifier can act on: `pairwise` is falsifiable by contradiction, `public` is observable, and everything between them is an unverifiable holder assertion, so splitting the middle gives a verifier two values it cannot tell apart.

A membership identifier is therefore `pairwise` when the community is its only counterparty, and `directed` when the member also uses it with other members. The join-time choice becomes a three-way one a person can actually be asked to make:

1. `pairwise` — known to the VTA only (**single-counterparty pseudonym**, lasting as long as the membership)
2. `directed` — known to the VTA and whoever the person chooses, including other members (**private persona**)
3. `public` — known to anyone (**public persona**)

### The four acronyms are retired

Not kept as informal shorthand. R-DID / M-DID / C-DID / P-DID leave the normative model *and* the glossary; their four term files are deleted. The shorthand is where the confusion lived. The 42 dangling references this would once have created are gone — the body no longer refers to the types at all.

## What the change moves rather than removes

Three things a community-bounded scope value was quietly carrying now have explicit homes:

**1. New normative subsection — "Scope the holder cannot declare alone."** A member can declare their membership identifier `pairwise`, but that stays truthful only if the community keeps it so: a VTC that publishes a member directory, or presents a member-issued VMC to a third party (which Privacy Consideration 8 permits), has widened the exposure without the member choosing it. So: **a VTC that issues VMCs MUST publish, in its governance framework or trust registry, whether member identifiers are disclosed beyond the VTA, and to whom** (bound on the VTC as an Issuer under Conformance Target 1), and a verifier MUST NOT infer from a member's `pairwise` declaration that the community treats it as such. This is what `community` appeared to capture — a property of the community, which belongs in its governance. A matching item is added to §Governance Considerations and to §Privacy Considerations.

**2. Intra-community relationships.** Under strict `pairwise` the identifier toward the VTC and the one toward a counterparty differ by construction, so the community-anchored ZKP must establish common control across two identifiers rather than read one out of both credentials. Stated in both §Correlation Scope and §Community-Anchored Zero-Knowledge Proof, along with the fact that `directed` is the honest default for intra-community use. The ZK protocols themselves remain out of scope, so this is not a new hole — it just stops being invisible.

**3. Durability and scope are chosen independently.** §DID Method Considerations no longer groups methods by VID type. A `pairwise` identifier toward a community must survive key rotation for the life of the membership, so "pairwise ⇒ disposable" is false. Durability follows the lifetime of the credentials issued under an identifier; scope follows the holder's disclosure choice; a method is judged against both.

## The uniqueness rule becomes a check

§Unilateral Relationship Identification currently requires *"each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for every single entity they connect with."* Under a declared scope that becomes the check #22 agreed: an identifier declared `pairwise` MUST NOT be used with more than one counterparty, a verifier that observes reuse MUST treat the declaration as false and MUST NOT rely on it, and implementations SHOULD default to a fresh identifier per relationship. `pairwise` is the one value falsifiable on evidence.

**The public community stops being an anomaly.** A community that wishes to be found declares `public` and is done. No bootstrapping exception, because `public` is an ordinary value on the axis rather than a departure from a pairwise default.

## What is deliberately unchanged

**Membership is still established by the VMC pair. A persona is still asserted by the VPC.** Those mechanisms have real machinery and it is untouched. Only the claim that the identifiers are distinct *types* is retired — which is the part that collides.

Mechanically, credential field constraints reduce to plain DIDs throughout: VRC, VMC, VIC, VPC and VWC no longer name identifier types in their issuer and subject rules. One exception is stated rather than implied — a witness identifier is `directed` at minimum, since it must be recognizable to both parties to the edge and to the community whose policy it is issued under.

## Where the declaration is carried: in the credential, by elimination

The first push left this open between the credential and the DID document. Review closed it on a technical fact rather than a preference: `did:key` and `did:peer` numalgo-0 documents are *derived* from the identifier value, so there is no document to add a property to — and those are exactly the methods §DID Method Considerations recommends for `pairwise` and `directed`. Encoding scope into a `did:peer:2` value would put the declaration into the identifier itself, which the section forbids a verifier from reading as a declaration. §Declaring scope now records option 1 and the two consequences that come with it (one scope per identifier across all its credentials; a first-party declaration covers only the issuer's own identifier, so the subject's scope in VPCs, VWCs, VICs and VECs is undeclared).

**Still open, deliberately:** the property name and `@context` term. Until they are named, the section binds a declaration that has been made and does not require one, so no credential is non-conforming for the absence of a declaration this version cannot yet carry. The examples carry none.

## Migration note

Implementations built against the first draft of #22 used a **four**-value vocabulary. The `ref-07-dtg-edge-semantics` fixtures in Keyring Wallet declare `community`, and that value does not map onto one scope: each `community` has to be re-decided as `pairwise` (the community is the only counterparty) or `directed` (the member also uses it with other members), per fixture. `rDid` is also a DIDComm wire field in the VRC reference implementation, so retiring the name there is a peer-compatibility change rather than a comment edit. The acronym rename is cheap; the re-decision is the substance of this change and no script can make it.

## Changed since the first push

- `community` dropped; `linked` renamed `directed` — per #41 and [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153).
- The four acronyms retired outright; `relationship_did.md`, `membership_did.md`, `community_did.md` and `persona_did.md` deleted rather than rewritten as shorthand.
- Added §Choosing a scope (informative — the three-way HTX choice, and when intentional correlation needs a ZK proof at all, per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5465297803)).
- Added §Scope the holder cannot declare alone (normative — the VTC disclosure requirement), with matching Governance and Privacy items.
- Added the durability-vs-scope rule to §DID Method Considerations.
- Credential field constraints reduced to plain DIDs; witness identifier stated as `directed` at minimum.
- Privacy Consideration 1 (M-DID reuse / migration) deleted; a new item covers what a community does with a member's identifier.
- `CONTEXT.md` updated so the repo's own vocabulary note no longer teaches the four types.

## Changed since review

Per [@bmiller59's review](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/30#issuecomment-5515992393) and the sequence in #31:

- **Rebased over #27 and #26.** #26's Edge Verifiability section is reworded from the retired vocabulary and gains one sentence naming the cross-VTN and no-VTN cases #24 asked for. #27's Privacy Consideration 9 is shortened to the one-line max-of-halves rule its description anticipated.
- **Item 1.** §Correlation Scope opens by binding only a declaration that has been made; a role may rule out declarations it would make false (the VTC and witness cases), stated in the section and in the `correlation scope` term; the VTC disclosure MUST binds the VTC as issuer, §Governance item 3 is a pointer, and Conformance Targets 1 and 3 pick up correlation scope.
- **Item 2.** The reuse check, as a plain normative paragraph in §Unilateral Relationship Identification; the "definitional rather than normative" paragraph is gone.
- **Item 3.** The ordering paragraph no longer contradicts the witness minimum; "ordered" replaces "monotonic" throughout.
- **Item 4.** Carriage settled on the credential, per the section above.
- **Item 5.** A supporting party — VWC witness, IDVP, resolver — is not a counterparty and does not widen scope.
- **Item 6.** The DID method sentence about the examples is now true, and the examples carry a note that the reused member identifier is `directed`.
- **Item 7.** §Roles are conferred by credentials is cut to the principle and the retired-acronym list.
- **Item 8.** `pairwise` is a single-counterparty pseudonym, not one-time; `public`'s intent column reads discoverability as a consequence.
- `directed` stays, per #41.

Spec-Up-T renders clean with no dangling references introduced.

## Related

- Implements [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22) — the structural proposal; carries the three-value resolution reached there.
- Carries the naming resolution from [dtgwg-cred-tf#41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41).
- [#21](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21) was closed by [#26](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/26), now on `main`; this PR rewords its Edge Verifiability section from the retired vocabulary.
- Closes [#23](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/23) together with [#27](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/27), now on `main` — an asymmetric edge is nameable once each half declares its own scope; §Scope the holder cannot declare alone states that a declaration binds only its own holder, and Privacy Consideration 9 states the max-of-halves rule.
- Supersedes the C-DID amendment in [#29](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29) and resolves its service-identifier editor's note — under a scope axis a mediator's identifier is simply `public`, with no new type needed. The two are otherwise independent.
- Independent of [#28](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/28), which reorders the credential-category sections. No overlap in substance — this PR does not touch the taxonomy — but both edit `spec/body.md` in the same neighbourhood, so whichever merges second will need a textual rebase.

title: Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method
body:
## Summary

Two related changes to how this specification treats DID methods.

**The examples showed `did:web` for durable issuers.** The VTC (`chess-club.example`), the witness service, and the IDVC issuer were all `did:web`. That method resolves to a document with no verifiable history: a verifier can establish which key is authoritative *now*, but not which key was authoritative *when the credential was signed*, and there is no recovery path on key compromise. Since DTG credentials may be presented long after issuance, and [Security Considerations](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#security-considerations) requires verifiers to validate the verification method, `did:web` understates what the specification assumes of a C-DID.

These examples now use [`did:webvh`](https://identity.foundation/didwebvh/), whose DID log publishes an append-only history of document versions, commits to successor keys via `nextKeyHashes`, and may be witnessed. Pairwise subjects are unchanged and stay on `did:key` / `did:peer`.

**The specification was silent on what it needs from a DID method.** It mandates none — correctly, and this PR does not change that — but it also never said what it relies on a method to provide, leaving implementers no basis for choosing one. The new informative `DID Method Considerations` subsection separates the two property sets, which pull against each other:

| | Durable (C-DID, M-DID) | Pairwise (R-DID, P-DID) |
|---|---|---|
| Key history | Verifiable, so signing-time key state is recoverable | Not required |
| Rotation | Without changing the identifier | Not required |
| Successor keys | Pre-rotation or equivalent commitment | Not required |
| Creation cost | Amortised over the identifier's life | Cheap, no registration step |
| Resolution origin | Independent of a single operator | **Not shared across identifiers** |
| Service endpoints | Discoverable (VTA, `credentialStatus`, trust registry) | Not required |

The conclusion is that implementations should expect to use more than one method rather than seeking one that serves every role. Nothing here requires an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` to share a method, and the examples now reflect that.

## Privacy consideration 7

Correlation does not require the credentials themselves. Where several of a party's R-DIDs or P-DIDs resolve through common infrastructure — a shared web origin, a shared registry, or a shared set of witnesses observing their updates — that infrastructure can associate identifiers the credential structure was designed to keep apart, and can observe when each is used.

The existing considerations (1–3) cover correlation through credential *content*; none covered correlation through the *resolution layer*. This makes DID method choice for pairwise roles a privacy decision, not only a key management one — and it is the reason the table above marks "no shared resolution origin" as the property that distinguishes the two sets.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Entirely informative.** No normative requirement is added, changed, or removed. No schema changes.
- **No method is mandated.** `did:webvh` appears in examples and as an illustration of a method satisfying the durable-role properties; the text is written in terms of properties so that other methods can be assessed against it. This is deliberate — it is what makes a later conformance statement for, say, a KERI-based method cheap to write.
- **SCIDs in the examples are illustrative placeholders**, truncated in the house style used elsewhere for `did:key` and `did:peer` values. They are not real, resolvable SCIDs.
- Independent of #19; the two touch different parts of the document.

title: VMC: allow a VTN's members to be VTCs or VTNs, and keep nested membership per-hop
body:
Proposed text for discussion #82 (VMC for VTN membership: members of a VTN are VTCs *and* VTNs). Please keep the substantive debate in the discussion; this PR is the concrete wording to react to.

## Changes

| # in #82 | Section | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | VMC Schema, VIC Schema | The subject of a VTN-issued VMC or VTN invitation may be a member VTC **or a member VTN**. |
| 2 | Membership Edge Completion | A VMC pair establishes membership only between its two parties. Membership MUST NOT be inferred through a chain of nested networks, and each pair is evaluated independently. |
| 4 | Edge Verifiability | When an anchor set is named as a VTN whose members include VTNs, the anchor set is expanded by verifier policy. That policy names the VTN, its framework version and the nesting depth, and counts completed memberships only. |
| 5 | Membership lifecycle editor's note | When the member is itself a VTC or VTN, its acknowledgement MAY carry a `credentialStatus` that it maintains. |
| — | Terms | **VTN**, **VTN member** and **VTN invitation credential** updated to match. |

**Item 3 in #82** (whether a one-sided listing is an unacknowledged VMC grant or a separate statement) was decided in the discussion as option (b): a listing is a VSC, not a grant. The predicates are [dtgwg-vsc-registry#33](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-vsc-registry/pull/33) (`lists/1`, `repudiates/1`, merged as drafts), and the VTI-VTN-013 wording is [dtgwg-vti-spec#94](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec/issues/94). This PR adds only an informative cross-reference to them (below).

## Verification

`npm run render` completes without errors (re-run after the rebase).

## Review changes (from #82)

- **VIC issuer:** a member VTN may issue a VTN invitation.
- **Membership Edge Completion:** it now cross-references Edge Verifiability, which permits traversal only as verifier policy. The long sentence is split.
- **Status:** the `credentialStatus` rule is moved out of the editor's note into normative text. It now requires a member-operated status list, and points to Security Considerations instead of duplicating it.
- **Direction:** the VMC subject reads "VTN-to-VTC or VTN-to-VTN".
- **Example:** a worked VMC pair where the member is a VTN.

**Consistent with item 3 of #82.** Edge Verifiability counts only *completed* memberships, while VTI-VTN-023 extends recognition to parties a VTN *lists*. Under option (b), which was adopted, the two line up: a listing is a separate `lists/1` statement, and an acknowledged listing is a completed pair.

## Since the review

- **Rebased onto main** after #74 and #86. The one conflict was the VIC `issuerScope` line: it keeps main's "`directed` at minimum" wording and this PR's "member VTC or member VTN" issuer line.
- **Example digest fixed:** the VTN-to-VTN acknowledgement's `digestMultibase` now reproduces from the grant as printed, per the spec's Digest Encoding section.
- **A listing is not a grant:** an informative note in Membership Edge Completion points to `lists/1` and `repudiates/1`, as requested in #82. It does not make them core profiles.

title: feat!: directed community grants, context-v3 salting (Working Draft 0.7.0)
body:
Implements DTG Core Credentials Working Draft 0.7.0 for the VTI Fig release.

### Directed community identifiers (trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#86)
A community-issued VMC declares `directed` at minimum, `public` where the community is open to outsiders. Only `pairwise` is refused now (`IssuerScopeTooNarrow { minimum: Directed }`, at parse and in `validate()`/`sign()`), and `new_member_vmc_for` acknowledges a `directed` grant.

**Breaking API:** `new_vmc(issuer, issuer_scope, subject, …)` and `new_community_role_vac(community, issuer_scope, member, …)` take the community's declaration. `new_community_role_vac` refuses `pairwise`. Pass `IssuerScope::Public` to keep the 0.15 behaviour. VIC docs state the same minimum. It isn't enforced there, because a VIC doesn't say whether its issuer is the community.

### Salting under context v3 (trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#87), behind `context-v3` (off by default)
The registry hasn't published `contexts/v3.jsonld`, and until its digest is recorded the spec says issuers MUST NOT emit `salt`. With the feature on:
- Constructors list `DTG_CONTEXT_V3` (`https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v3`) and draw a 32-byte base58btc `z…` salt in `build()`, not in `sign()`, so a re-proof keeps it (including signing via another backend after `validate()`) and a re-issue redraws it.
- A parse accepts v3 only with a salt that decodes to exactly 32 bytes (`InvalidSalt`).
- `with_purposes` keeps v3.

In every build, feature on or off, a `salt` under v1/v2 is refused (`InvalidSalt`). Before this change it passed through `DTGCommon::extra`. The crate has no selective-disclosure path, and the field docs say `salt` must be mandatory-disclosure.

The salt is drawn with `rand` 0.10. It's already in the normal dependency graph through the affinidi crates and is now an optional dependency of the feature, so the feature adds no new crate.

### Docs
- README now states Working Draft 0.7.0: contexts v1 and v2 supported, v3 pending.
- New *Salting (context v3)* section.
- 0.16 upgrade row: upgrade verifiers before issuers emit `directed`, and before any issuer enables `context-v3`.
- CHANGELOG entry under Unreleased.
- "member VTC" now reads VTC or VTN (trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#83).

### Tests
- `tests/salt.rs` covers v1/v2 salt refusal in every build, v3 unrecognized when the feature is off, v3 issue/parse, fresh salt per issue, refusal of a missing, short, long or wrong-base salt, salted acknowledgement, and re-proof keeping the salt.
- New scope tests: directed and public grants accepted, pairwise refused, acknowledging a directed grant, and the directed role VAC verifying while a pairwise one is refused.
- The golden v1 wire-form tests are gated to builds without `context-v3`.

body:
Bumps `_Document Status:_` from `Working Draft 0.6.0` to `Working Draft 0.7.0`. One line in `spec/header.md`; nothing else changes.

## Why MINOR

Document Status was last set in #68. Since then these have merged without a bump:

| PR | Change | Class under Compatibility Rules |
|---|---|---|
| #84 | A VAC may state `purposes` | Backward-compatible |
| #86 | A VTC's identifier may be `directed` | Backward-compatible (relaxes a constraint) |
| #74 | Correlation Scope reworked as a controller's declaration | Normative rewording |
| #90 | A VTC MUST publish, show and keep to its disclosure practice | Breaking (a SHOULD becomes a MUST; new MUST NOTs) |
| #91 | Relationship Admissibility | Backward-compatible (new SHOULDs) |
| #87 | `salt` REQUIRED under context `v3` | Breaking (adds a REQUIRED property; dormant until `v3` is published) |
| #83 | A VTN's members may be VTCs or VTNs | Backward-compatible, with new verifier MUST NOTs |
| #89 | Attenuated VAC example digest | Editorial |

Per [Compatibility Rules](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/blob/main/spec/intro.md), a breaking change before first ratification is released as a MINOR increment, and MAJOR stays at `0`. So the batch is one MINOR step, with PATCH reset to `0`.

## Follow-up

#87 left its own bump to the release that records the `v3` context digest. That release would be the next increment after this one.

VMC: allow a VTN's members to be VTCs or VTNs, and keep nested membership per-hop (#83)

* VMC: allow a VTN's members to be VTCs or VTNs, and keep nested membership per-hop

Proposed text for discussion #82. A VTN can list other networks
(nested state -> national -> global networks), but the VMC and VIC
subject rules only named a member VTC.

- VMC and VIC subject: a member VTC or a member VTN.
- Membership Edge Completion: a VMC pair establishes membership only
  between its two parties; membership is not inferred through a chain
  of nested networks, and each pair is evaluated independently.
- Edge Verifiability: an anchor set named as a VTN whose members
  include VTNs is expanded by verifier policy naming the VTN, its
  framework version and the nesting depth, counting completed
  memberships only.
- Membership lifecycle note: a member that is itself a VTC or VTN may
  carry credentialStatus on its acknowledgement, since it already runs
  a status mechanism under its own control.
- Terms: VTN, VTN member and VTN invitation credential updated to match.

The listing-vs-grant ordering question raised in #82 is left open for
the discussion and is not changed here.

title: Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated
body:
Closes #38.

Implements the placement agreed on #38 (stormer78's 25 Sep proposal, +1 from bmiller59, matching ZKP record 022): one top-level `salt` inside every credential's hashed block, so every digest that references the credential is blinded at once.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **Base Structure:** new `salt` member: REQUIRED under context `v3` and later, absent under `v1`/`v2`; exactly 32 bytes from a CSPRNG, fresh per credential, never reused or derived, base-58-btc multibase. Kept on re-proof, redrawn on re-issue. Mandatory-disclosure under selective-disclosure suites. Verifiers reject a `v3` credential with a missing or malformed salt. The `@context` bullet now admits later context versions (it already had to, for `v2`).
- **Context Versions:** `v3` = `v2` + `salt`; once its digest is recorded, every credential lists `v3` or later. Editor's note (same pattern as #84): `v3` isn't published yet, so issuers MUST NOT emit `salt` until it is, and examples move to `v3` when the digest is recorded.
- **Digest Encoding:** the "none of these is salted" editor's note becomes a **Salting** subsection: why, a salted grant + acknowledgement example whose `digestMultibase` reproduces from the grant as printed (and the unsalted digest for contrast), and what a salt does *not* do: presentation linkability, `taskDigestMultibase` (going away under #58), and VSC `predicate` blinding stay with ZKP work. Profile-defined digests: SHOULD reference something salted or say why enumeration isn't a concern.
- **Vetting profile** and the **ZK editor's note** updated to point at the new subsection.
- **`CONTEXT.md`:** Salt entry.

### Follow-ups
- **Registry:** `dtgwg-vsc-registry` needs a `v3` context (= `v2` + a plain-string `salt` term) per GOVERNANCE §3.1; then a small PR records the digest, drops the editor's note and moves the examples to `v3` with salts (several example digests will change then).
- **`nodeType` (#53)** could join `v3` if its value list is settled first.
- No Document Status bump here; leaving that for the release that records `v3`.

Rendered with `npm run render`: no errors, and all in-page links resolve.

title: Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated (#87)
body:
Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated (#87)

* Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated

Every digest-valued reference (the acknowledgement, the acceptance, a
statement's object, and the VDC/VAC chain parents) hashes a credential
whose content is often guessable, so an observer shown only the digest
can recover who joined what by trying candidates.

- Base Structure: a top-level salt, REQUIRED under context v3 and later
  and absent under v1/v2: 32 fresh CSPRNG bytes, base-58-btc multibase,
  kept on re-proof and redrawn on re-issue, mandatory-disclosure under
  selective-disclosure suites. The @context bullet admits later versions.
- Context Versions: v3 is v2 plus salt; once its digest is recorded every
  credential lists v3 or later. An editor's note says v3 is unpublished
  and issuers must not emit salt until it is.
- Digest Encoding: the enumeration editor's note becomes a Salting
  subsection with a salted grant/acknowledgement pair whose digest
  reproduces, what a salt does not do (presentation linkability,
  taskDigestMultibase, VSC predicate), and a SHOULD for profile-defined
  digests.
- Vetting profile and the ZK editor's note follow the new subsection.
- CONTEXT.md: a Salt entry.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Salting: restore the context-copy recommendation; cover unsalted credentials

- Move "Verifiers SHOULD use a local copy of each context" back out of
  the temporary v3 editor's note into the body text
- Context Versions: the v1/v2 allowances hold only until v3 is recorded
- Say what to do with v1/v2 credentials once v3 is recorded: a party
  SHOULD decline to reference an unsalted credential, and a verifier
  SHOULD NOT accept a later-dated credential that lists v1 or v2
- Note that the salt is itself a linking value, including under
  otherwise unlinkable selective-disclosure suites
- Note that disclosing the salt is necessary but not sufficient for a
  derived credential to match a digest

title: Ask a VTC to publish which VRC subjects it admits
body:
Closes #25. **Stacked on #74** (base is #74's branch) so it builds on the reworked correlation-scope text; it retargets to `main` when #74 merges. It doesn't touch the lines #90 changes, and the two merge cleanly together.

Based on geoffturk's proposed text on #25 (7 Sep), with his three open questions answered as follows. Reviewers can push back on any of them:

1. **SHOULD, not MUST, on publication.** A failed cross-community edge is a policy outcome, not a conformance failure. The disclosure-practice requirement is a MUST because without it a member's `pairwise` declaration becomes false; nothing equivalent breaks here.
2. **Subject side only.** The failure case in #25 is about the subject. The issuer's own scope is already declared in `issuerScope` on the credential.
3. **The ordering sentence stays, briefly.** It states the intended ordering and leaves the exchange to the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols spec, with no mechanism defined here.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **New `#### Relationship Admissibility`** at the end of Edge Verifiability (the alternative location geoffturk suggested, which keeps it clear of #90's edits). A VTC whose members issue VRCs SHOULD publish the correlation scopes it accepts for VRC subjects and whether it admits non-member subjects. A VTA SHOULD show a counterparty community's answer before a member issues their half. It states the intended ordering, and that a policy-hiding (ZK) form of mutual admissibility is out of scope (mitchuski's note on #25).
- **Governance Considerations item 10:** these are governance determinations, and publishing them is what makes the pre-flight check possible.

title: Bind a VTC to the disclosure practice it publishes
body:
Closes #81. **Stacked on #74**: the base is #74's branch, because the text lives in the subsection #74 renames ("A scope the controller cannot declare alone"). Once #74 merges, GitHub retargets this to `main`.

Implements the three suggested changes from #81, all in that subsection:

- **A. Pre-join notice is a MUST.** The VTC publishes its *disclosure practice* (whether member identifiers go beyond the VTA, to whom, and whether that depends on declared scope), and the VTA MUST show it before a prospective member chooses a scope.
- **B. The VTC is held to it.** A VTC MUST NOT disclose a member's identifier beyond the practice published when that member joined. A changed practice applies only to members who join or re-acknowledge after the change, and the VTA MUST tell a member before they re-acknowledge.
- **C. A third option.** A VTC MAY publish that it *respects declared scope*: it then MUST NOT disclose a `pairwise` or `directed` member identifier beyond the VTA (directory, presenting the acknowledgement, or otherwise), and MAY disclose a `public` one.

The verifier rule ("MUST NOT infer from a `pairwise` declaration…") is kept, since none of this is checkable from the credentials.

Follow-on edits:
- **Membership lifecycle editor's note:** "withdrawal of consent is self-sovereign" now says it is in the member's hands but all-or-nothing, and does not by itself stop the community disclosing an identifier it already holds (the Exit Rights point in #81).
- **Privacy Considerations item 8:** presenting the acknowledgement to a third party is bounded by the published practice, and a scope-respecting VTC doesn't do it for `pairwise`/`directed` members.
- **Governance Considerations item 3:** updated to match.

Not in scope here (#81's "food for thought"): consent before a VTC presents an acknowledgement, a member-controlled status mechanism, and a ZK acknowledgement form. Those belong to the Trust Task protocols and ZKP specs.

title: Bind a VTC to the disclosure practice it publishes (#90)
body:
Bind a VTC to the disclosure practice it publishes (#90)

* Bind a VTC to the disclosure practice it publishes

A member's pairwise or directed declaration toward a VTC stays truthful
only if the VTC keeps it so, but the VTC only had to publish its practice,
the VTA only SHOULD show it before the member chose a scope, and nothing
held the VTC to it afterwards.

- The VTA MUST show the published disclosure practice before a
  prospective member chooses a scope.
- A VTC MUST NOT disclose a member's identifier beyond the practice
  published when that member joined; a changed practice applies only to
  members who join or re-acknowledge afterwards, after being told.
- A VTC MAY publish that it respects declared scope, and then keeps
  pairwise and directed member identifiers with the VTA.
- Membership lifecycle note: withdrawal is in the member's hands but
  all-or-nothing, rather than "self-sovereign".
- Privacy item 8 and Governance item 3 follow.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Hold the VTC, not the VTA, to the disclosure-practice duties

- The pre-join notice and the change notice now bind the VTC, which
  ordinarily meets them through its VTA; a VTA is not a conformance
  target
- Conformance Targets: a VTC issuing VMCs publishes its practice, makes
  it available to prospective members, and keeps to it
- Each published version of a practice SHOULD be dated and SHOULD stay
  available after it is superseded
- State what a changed practice means for a member: re-acknowledgement
  can be forced, declining ends the membership, and a different scope
  means a new identifier
- Privacy Considerations item 3: a VTC states its practice and keeps to
  it

title: Cryptographic review of 18 November folded: record 025 reworked, records 007, 009, 022, 024 amended
body:
Folds the cryptographic review of records 007, 009, 022, 024 and 025 (#25). Every point is taken. Record 025 moves to `constructed` (second commit); no other record changes state. Evidence revision pinned in Appendix B: [`7cc658e`](https://github.com/mitchuski/dtgwg-zkp-mage/commit/7cc658e89c8f).

### Record 025 — reworked

As first specified the rotation proof needed the current secret, so a lost secret could not be replaced although the record's stated need covers loss; and the replacement leaf took a fresh revocation handle, so a member could rotate out of reach of revocation.

- The enrolment leaf is `Com(H(s), N, ρ; r)`: the image of the presenting secret, the pre-rotation digest `N = Hpre(H(s′))`, the revocation handle.
- Clauses 3 and 4: the rotation is authorised by the pre-committed next secret `s′`, which opens `L′`. The retiring leaf is opened by `H(s)`, so `s` is not a witness. A lost `s` rotates; a stolen `s` alone cannot.
- Clause 5 (new, record 009): `L′` carries the same handle `ρ`, proven equal without disclosing it. Revocation survives the rotation.
- The spent-tag set is committed over strictly sorted tags, as record 006 requires of `rl_root`; records 010, 023 and 024 name `spent_root` as a public input.
- Formal model rebuilt: `next_secret_fixed`, `handle_carried_forward`, `revocation_survives_rotation`, and `fresh_handle_escapes` as the counter-deployment for the earlier relation. Knowledge of `s′` is knowledge soundness and stays outside the model.

### Second commit — the circuit, and what building it found

- The rotation is built in the evidence repository: `runtimes/circom-gadget/circuits/rotation.circom`, one circuit, 11,987 constraints, six public signals, about 1.3 s to prove and 21 ms to verify, 320 B with compressed points; lab-only setup. Thirteen fixtures pass, among them: a witness built with no presenting secret among the inputs; a stolen presenting secret that cannot rotate; a replacement under another handle refused; a member revoked after rotating who cannot rotate again.
- Building it corrected clause 3. The first commit kept the pre-rotation digest over the whole next leaf, `N = H(L′)`. That leaf carries its own digest over the leaf after it, so the first leaf can never be minted. The digest now commits to the next secret's image, as a key event log commits to the next key, and the replacement leaf is minted at the rotation.
- Record 006's sorted-neighbour clause gets its first runtime, as a template in the same circuit: range leaves, one inclusion proof, two 128-bit comparisons. One fixture commits an unsorted list and shows a revoked handle passing, which is the registry's duty the proof cannot check.
- Not built: the presentation side of a rotation-capable profile (the tag-absence clause against `spent_root`).

### Records 007, 009, 022, 024 — amended

- **007**: the quantum-confidentiality line corrected (a hash commitment is computationally hiding; a SNARK-native key gives up `s` to Shor); salt distinctness and hardened derivation at issuance; knowledge of an opening separated from control of the DID.
- **009**: canonical form and injective encoding of the compared value; verification under a hidden issuer recorded as an open requirement of records 020 and 021 (one line each); the colluding-issuer claim narrowed.
- **022**: the relation restated for the adopted in-credential salt, `H(JCS(credential incl. salt))`; mandatory disclosure of the salt under selective-disclosure suites found to reopen the enumeration (raised on cred-spec PR #87); in-circuit JSON reading named as a risk.
- **024**: the anonymity claim stated over the non-colluding vetters; a stated policy and a k − 1 reading for self-attestation in the Groth16 route; option 1's assumptions; a profile's setup requirement.
- **007, 009, 022** and Public Input Conventions: the transcript binding is record 003's clause; a declared but unconstrained `transcriptDigest` is not bound.

### Chapters

Integration (rotation under the identifier commitment profile, WG-17), Security Considerations (trusted setup), Appendix D changelog, the WG-15 and WG-17 rows.

### Checks

`validate` 24/24, `test` pass, render clean. Formal gate in the evidence repository: 19 records, 70 clauses, 79 roots and 37 review-witness theorems within the standard axioms, `leanchecker --fresh` clean; sealed root `sha256:6e963611fcdd91dfc0e2f1ec6f6ad8e3d70b2f9cd07e404bb8bef6e95eb6464d`. Circuit: `node test-rotation.mjs`, 13/13.

### Open for a second reading (WG-17)

- Custody of the rotation material: `s′` and the opening of `L` kept apart from `s`, or all of it derived from `s′`.
- Whether the rotation tag should key on `H(s)` as written.

Answers #25, which stays open for the reviewer's second reading of 025.

title: vtc-audit-v0.5.0
body: ### Added - **vtc-service**: Store and serve an uploaded community logo ([#2751](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2751)) * feat(vtc-service): store and serve an uploaded community logo A community can now upload its logo, and the VTC serves it from its own origin, so it shows in the console, the member portal, both sign-in pages and the default landing page wherever the VTC is hosted. Before this, the logo was only the profile's `logoUrl`. Those pages are served with `img-src 'self' data:`, so a logo at any other address was never drawn, and a deployment with nowhere on the VTC's own origin to put a file (a hosted VTC, say) had no logo at all: a filesystem website must have its own host, and `admin_ui.members_dir` is a snapshot that stops following the daemon on every upgrade. What it adds: - `vtc/community/logo/update/0.1` (pinned in `vti-specs-vtc`): an administrator (`vtc.surface.admin`) sends a PNG, JPEG or WebP, or `image: null` to remove the logo. The community re-encodes it as a PNG of at most 512 px (`directory::images::reencode_logo`, sharing the directory's decoding and its bounds), dropping all metadata and any bytes after the image data, and stores it in the `community` keyspace, which is backed up. 20 changes per administrator per hour, one re-encoding at a time, audited as `CommunityLogoUpdated` by digest. - `GET /v1/community/logo`: public, like `public-profile`. Served from memory against a small record read, with a fixed `Content-Type`, `nosniff`, `default-src 'none'; sandbox`, an `ETag` and `304`. Bytes that do not match their record are never served. - A `logo` member (`url`, `sha256`, `mediaType`, `width`, `height`) on the public profile and on `/v1/member/me`'s `community`. Every page draws it in preference to `logoUrl`, which is unchanged. - Console: a Logo card on the Community profile page. It rasterizes an SVG in the browser, from a `data:` URL inside an `` where it runs no script, so no SVG is ever sent or stored. The Logo URL field now says when these pages will not draw the address it holds. Design note: docs/05-design-notes/vtc-community-logo.md.
